articles.title: New study finds bosses who brag about their own good deeds risk disgusting their employees
articles.summary: A manager who talks about their own fairness and compassion can inspire employees or come across as self-righteous. New research across 254 workplace pairs and a controlled experiment suggests the difference lies in whether the boss also credits others.

articles.title: Psychedelics trigger a bizarre memory paradox that makes the unknown feel like home
articles.summary: Psychedelic trips feel strikingly new. Yet users often describe arriving somewhere they already know. A new study suggests this paradoxical familiarity differs from both everyday déjà vu and cherished personal memories.

articles.title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.18642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. articles.title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.18747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior.

articles.summary: arXiv:2611.18598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences. articles.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
articles.summary: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.

articles.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

articles.title: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts
articles.summary: A massive study involving more than 415,000 Americans has uncovered a concerning connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts. Researchers found that adults with the disorder had 57% higher odds of experiencing suicidal thoughts, with women and younger adults facing particularly elevated risks.

articles.title: Scientists who use AI propose less distinctive ideas for federal research grants
articles.summary: A new study of U.S. federal grant applications suggests that scientists using generative AI tend to pitch research closer to previously funded topics. At the NIH, AI-heavy proposals won funding more often and preceded modestly more routine papers.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex?
